title: Quick start
intro.1: From a fresh Linux server to a watched browser session in a few minutes: nothing is compiled on the server.
1-install-it.title: 1. Install it
1-install-it.1: You need Linux on x86-64 with systemd and Docker Engine 28 or newer, with Compose and Buildx. Ask your coding agent on the server:
1-install-it.2: Or run the installer yourself, after reading it:
1-install-it.3: It runs as your own account, which only has to be in the docker group: no sudo. The firewall rule and the TCP settings below are made as root through a short-lived privileged container of Debian’s image, pulled by its digest, whose nsenter runs the server’s own iptables, systemctl and sysctl (Docker must allow such a container). In order, it:
1-install-it.4: checks the server: Docker, memory, disk and port 9443 (TCP and UDP);
1-install-it.5: clones easi.run into ~/easi.run at the release it names;
1-install-it.6: puts the firewall rule that keeps pages off the server’s own services in place, and makes Docker put it back before every start, so Docker and its containers start only once it is there;
1-install-it.7: when the kernel has BBR, sets the server’s TCP to pace with fq and BBR and not to slow down after a pause, for viewers far away (see Operations), keeping the values it replaces for --uninstall to put back;
1-install-it.8: pulls the images easi.run’s CI built from that release, each checked against the digest the installer names (about 350 MB), and adds Google’s current Chrome stable to the browser image from Google’s signed repository (about 150 MB): Google’s terms let no one else ship Chrome. On 2 cores with a fast connection, this takes one to two minutes;
1-install-it.9: starts easi.run, and checks it over HTTPS against the admin’s own certificate;
1-install-it.10: offers easi.run to Claude Code over MCP (see Agents);
1-install-it.11: prints a summary: whether the admin’s password is set, whether MCP is ready, and the lines for another computer, the SSH tunnel’s among them.
1-install-it.12: bash install.sh --dry-run runs the checks and lists the images it would pull, changing nothing; bash install.sh --update, with a newer installer, moves an installation to its release.
2-open-it.title: 2. Open it
2-open-it.1: The admin is at https://localhost:9443, on the server’s 127.0.0.1 only. From your computer, use the command you already use to log in to the server, adding -N -L 9443:127.0.0.1:9443, and keep it running; then open https://localhost:9443. For example:
2-open-it.2: The installer’s summary prints this line, filled in with your login when it can tell it. VS Code and Cursor over Remote-SSH forward the port for you: open the link from their terminal, or add port 9443 in their Ports view; either way, the local port must be 9443 too.
2-open-it.3: The certificate is self-signed: the installer keeps a copy in ~/.config/easi-run/tls-cert.pem, and the admin logs its SHA-256 fingerprint at start, so you can check it before you accept it.
3-create-your-password.title: 3. Create your password and start a session
3-create-your-password.1: Open https://localhost:9443 (from your computer, through the tunnel) right after the install: until a password is set, the admin’s first screen asks for one. Choose it, 12 characters or more; you are logged in at once.
3-create-your-password.2: Next, add a second step at sign-in, or skip it for now. It is optional, and we suggest it: with it on, your password alone opens nothing. An authenticator app works in every browser: scan the QR code, type the 6-digit code it shows, and each code signs in once. A passkey, where your browser offers one, signs you in on its own with your fingerprint, face or device PIN; Chrome offers none on a site whose certificate it does not trust, such as the server’s own over the tunnel, and the page then says so. Save the ten recovery codes it shows once: if you lose your phone or passkey, sign in with your password and one of them; each works once. Change it later under Security.
3-create-your-password.3: Type a URL and press Start session, or ask your agent to open one.
3-create-your-password.4: Open the session: when nobody holds control and no agent is using the session (no call running, none ended in the last 30 seconds), you usually hold control at once (The agent lists every case); otherwise you watch and take it with the control (cursor) button in the session’s bar, which also hands it back to the agent.
without-the-installer.title: Without the installer
without-the-installer.1: First, the firewall rule, which keeps pages off the services on every address the host holds (see Security). Keep it across reboots with your host’s firewall configuration.
without-the-installer.3: Then open https://localhost:9443 and choose your password, 12 characters or more. DOCKER_GID gives the controller the group of the Docker socket; without it, no session can start.
without-the-installer.4: Each browser session gets 2 CPUs and 2048 MiB by default. The installer runs as many at once as the server’s memory holds (one on 4 GB, two on 8 GB, four on 16 GB, up to 16); by hand, one runs at once. Change that with BROWSER_CPUS, BROWSER_MEMORY_MIB and ADMIN_MAX_SESSIONS; see Configuration.
